title: How to Plan for Retirement When Your Spouse Has No Savings
description: Strategies for single-earner or financially unequal couples.
content:
It is common for one spouse to handle the earning and investing while the other manages the home or works a job without benefits. This creates a lopsided balance sheet where one partner holds all the assets. In a healthy marriage, this is 'Our Money,' but legally and logistically, it requires specific planning. You need to ensure the non-saving spouse is protected against the death of the earner, and that the household savings rate is high enough to support two people on one portfolio.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Double Burden': The earning spouse must save enough for *two* retirements. The standard '15% savings rate' is for one person. A sole earner needs to save 20-25% of their gross income to fund a couple's retirement.
  • Spousal IRA: The IRS allows a working spouse to contribute to an IRA (Traditional or Roth) in the name of a non-working spouse. This effectively doubles your annual tax-advantaged space ($14,000 total).
  • Survivor Benefits: Social Security and Pensions have survivor options. You must choose the 'Joint and Survivor' payout on pensions, even if it lowers the monthly check, to ensure the non-earner isn't destitute if the earner dies first.
  • Life Insurance Bridge: If the earner dies before retirement, the savings stop. You need a large Term Life policy on the earner to replace the future savings they would have accumulated.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Social Security Spousal Benefits guarantee the lower-earning spouse 50% of the higher earner's benefit (while both are alive) and 100% of the higher earner's benefit (after the earner dies). Maximizing the earner's record is the priority.

The Protection Checklist

Ensure the non-saver is safe.

1. The 'Our Money' Meeting

Stop saying 'My 401(k)'. It is 'Our Retirement'.
Action: Review beneficiaries. The spouse must be the primary beneficiary on all 401(k)s and IRAs. (Federal law mandates this for 401ks unless waived).

2. The Spousal IRA

Limit: $7,000/year ($8,000 if 50+).
Strategy: Open a Roth IRA in the non-working spouse's name. Max it out every January.
Why: This builds assets in their name, providing autonomy and tax diversification.

3. Social Security Timing

The earner must delay until 70.
Reason: The survivor benefit is based on when the earner claimed. If earner claims at 62, the widow gets a small check for life. If earner claims at 70, the widow gets a max check for life.

Household Budgeting

  1. Calculate Joint Needs: A couple needs ~$75,000/year for a comfortable retirement. Social Security might cover $45,000. The Portfolio must cover $30,000.
  2. The Savings Target: To generate $30,000/yr, you need $750,000 invested. Can the single earner hit this? If not, you need to cut expenses or work longer.
  3. Catch-Up Contributions: If the earner is 50+, they can put $30,500 into a 401(k). This large bucket is essential for single-income households catching up.
  4. Long-Term Care: The non-earning spouse (often female) statistically lives longer and is more likely to need nursing care. Ensure the plan has a 'LTC Fund' so she isn't left broke at age 85.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if we divorce?

Retirement assets accumulated during marriage are generally split 50/50 (QDRO). However, the non-earner stops accumulating new savings. Divorce is financially devastating for the non-saver.

Does the non-earner get Medicare?

Yes. If the working spouse has 40 quarters of coverage, the non-working spouse qualifies for Medicare Part A (Free) at age 65 on their record.

Should the non-earner work part-time?

Yes. Even earning $15,000/year allows them to max their own IRA and adds to the household safety net. It also builds their own Social Security credits.
